summary: Defines a YANG module for configuring In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM) functions. IOAM is an on-path hybrid measurement method; its data fields are discussed in RFC 9197 and RFC 9326.

plainLanguage.summary: IOAM lets packets record their journey. This gives a standard settings form to turn it on across network devices.

questions: what are the ioam profile types
subtitle: A standard configuration schema for switching on IOAM, the method that lets packets collect telemetry on the path they travel.

tldr.problem: In situ OAM (IOAM) records operational and telemetry data inside or alongside packets, but each vendor would otherwise need its own way to configure which flows are measured and what is recorded.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9617 defines the YANG module ietf-ioam. It holds a list of named profiles, each tying a flow filter and a carrier protocol to up to five IOAM options: incremental trace, pre-allocated trace, direct export, proof of transit and edge-to-edge.
tldr.outcome: Operators can configure IOAM on devices through NETCONF or RESTCONF with one vendor-independent data model. It only covers configuration; the data fields themselves are defined elsewhere.

today: RFC 9617 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2024. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What IOAM and This Model Are For
sections.content:
In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM) is an on-path hybrid measurement method. It produces operational and telemetry information that can be exported in-band or out-of-band. The data types and formats of the IOAM data records come from RFC 9197 and RFC 9326, and the data can ride in encapsulations such as the Network Service Header (RFC 9452) and IPv6.

RFC 9617 does not define those data fields. It defines a YANG data model, the module ietf-ioam, for configuring IOAM capabilities. YANG is the data modeling language of RFC 7950. The model supports five IOAM options: Incremental Trace, Pre-allocated Trace, Direct Export, Proof of Transit (POT) and Edge-to-Edge.
sections.plainLanguage: Other documents say what a packet can write in its travel diary. This one only says how a network engineer fills in the form that turns the diary on.

sections.title: Structure of the Model
sections.content:
The model is organized as a list of profiles. Each profile is tied to one flow and the IOAM information for it. At the top, ioam holds three containers.

  • info is read-only. It holds the timestamp type and the list of available interfaces, which help monitoring systems interpret the IOAM data.
  • admin-config holds the enabled flag. When it is true, IOAM configuration is enabled for the system and the IOAM data plane functionality is enabled. The module text says it MUST be set to true before anything under the profile list can be edited, and that if it is false, configuration in place is not used.
  • profiles holds the list of profiles, keyed by profile-name.

The model conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) of RFC 8342. It reuses the ACL module of RFC 8519, the interfaces module of RFC 8343 and the ietf-lime-time-types module of RFC 8532.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a main switch, a read-only noticeboard that shows what the device can do, and a list of recipes. Each recipe says which packets to watch and what to record.

sections.title: Filters, Carrier Protocols and Features
sections.content:
Each profile has a filter that identifies the flow the profile applies to. Access Control Lists (RFC 8519) are the common way to describe a flow: a profile can refer to an Access Control Entry (ACE) by name, and when the matched ACE forwarding action is accept, IOAM actions MUST be driven by the accepted packets.

The protocol-type says where IOAM is applied. The module defines the identities ipv6 (see RFC 9486) and nsh (see RFC 9452). With ipv6, the IOAM ingress node encapsulates the flow according to RFC 9486.

A configured device may not support every option. Five YANG features show which are supported: incremental-trace, preallocated-trace, direct-export, proof-of-transit and edge-to-edge. Several IOAM data types can be encapsulated into the same IOAM header in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: A recipe first says which packets it is about, like "all parcels for this street". Then it says which kind of envelope carries the diary. Each device only offers the diary types it knows how to keep.

sections.title: The Five Profiles
sections.content:
Each profile can hold one sub-profile per IOAM option. Sub-profiles are containers that exist only when configured (they carry a presence statement).

  • Pre-allocated trace (Section 3.2): the encapsulating node pre-allocates space in the packet for every node on the path to fill in. Settings are node-action, trace-types (a namespace plus a list of trace types) and max-length, the maximum length of the node data list in octets.
  • Incremental trace (Section 3.3): each node allocates and pushes its node data right after the option header. It has the same settings as the pre-allocated profile.
  • Direct export (Section 3.4): a trigger for IOAM data to be exported directly or aggregated locally without being pushed into in-flight packets. It adds flow-id, used to correlate exported data of the same flow from multiple nodes and packets, and enable-sequence-number, which is off by default.
  • Proof of transit (Section 3.5): supports path or service function chain verification. It has a namespace and a pot-type. To align with RFC 9197 only POT type 0 is defined, and users must augment the module for other types.
  • Edge-to-edge (Section 3.6): carries data added by the encapsulating node and interpreted by the decapsulating node. It has node-action and e2e-types.

The node-action is one of three identities: encapsulate, transit or decapsulate the IOAM header. It defaults to action-transit. The trace types, max-length, flow-id and edge-to-edge types are only meaningful on the encapsulating node.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five kinds of diary. Some are filled in by every stop along the trip, one is sent straight to a collector, one proves the trip happened, and one is just a note from the start to the end.

sections.title: Configuration Examples
sections.content:
The appendices show NETCONF edit-config messages in XML, one per profile type.

  • Incremental trace: an ingress node encapsulates IOAM in the IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option header, captures transit delay at each node, and keeps the node data list at no more than 512 bytes.
  • Pre-allocated trace: the ingress node selects the flow with the ACL test-acl, encapsulates in the NSH, collects namespace-specific data in short format and pre-allocates 512 bytes.
  • Direct export and edge-to-edge: an egress node with action-decapsulate detects the option in the IPv6 extension header and removes it, cleaning all the IOAM data.
  • Proof of transit: the node applies POT type 0 with IPv6 encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples are filled-in forms, so you can see what a real recipe looks like for each kind of diary.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is meant to be accessed with NETCONF or RESTCONF. Their mandatory-to-implement secure transports are SSH (RFC 6242) for NETCONF and TLS (RFC 8446) for RESTCONF. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations and content.

Writable data nodes can be sensitive. Unexpected changes under /ioam/admin-config could disrupt IOAM functions or cause misbehaving profiles. Unexpected changes under /ioam/profiles/profile could cause incorrect IOAM behavior for the matching flows, which would affect performance monitoring, data analytics and related services.

Read access matters too. The profile subtree might reveal information about services deployed for customers, so a customer who is allowed to monitor their own services should only see nodes for those services.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted people should be allowed to change or read the settings, because wrong settings break the measurements and the settings can reveal who uses what.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has registered the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-ioam in the IETF XML Registry. It has also registered the module in the YANG Module Names registry with the name ietf-ioam and the prefix ioam, referencing RFC 9617.
sections.plainLanguage: The module got an official name in the public list of YANG modules so nobody else uses the same one.
